original_interpretation: TSMC said pricing gains in recent years only just covered inflation in tools, equipment, materials and labour.
evidence_found: "in the last few years the pricing benefits to the profitability was just enough to cover the inflation cost from tools, equipment, materials, labor, etc." (CFO Wendell Huang, 4Q25 call, Yahoo Finance transcript at 1:03:14; same words in TickerTrends transcript)
notes: Two independent transcripts agree word for word. The TSMC IR PDF (SRC-0025) could only be read up to about 50k characters, and this Q&A passage falls after that point. TickerTrends names the speaker 'Jen-Chau Huang'; Yahoo names Wendell Huang (CFO). Correctly typed as reported_claim.

original_interpretation: C.C. Wei said in Jan 2026 that TSMC Arizona's yield and defect density are almost equal to Taiwan's.
evidence_found: "We built a fab in Arizona, and we worked hard, so today, everything, even the yield or defect density is almost equal to Taiwan." (C.C. Wei, 4Q25 call, 15 Jan 2026, TSMC IR edited transcript)
notes: Checked against TSMC's own IR transcript (SRC-0025). Original source added via updates. This is the company's own claim and no yield data is given (reported_claim).

original_interpretation: TSMC guided 2026 depreciation up by a high-teens percentage YoY, mainly from the 2nm ramp.
evidence_found: "Our deprecation expense is expected to increase by a high-teens percentage year-over-year in 2026, mainly as we ramp up our two-nanometer technologies." (CFO prepared remarks, 4Q25 call, TSMC IR transcript)
notes: This is company guidance (a forecast), not an actual result. IR original added as a source.

original_interpretation: Morris Chang said in April 2022 that chips from TSMC's Oregon fab cost 50% more than Taiwan's, and that years of effort had not narrowed the gap much.
evidence_found: "While a few years of effort did improve the factory's performance, the difference in cost between the US and Taiwan remains almost the same, he added. Chips made at the Oregon factory cost 50 percent more than those make TSMC's factories in Taiwan, Chang said." (Taipei Times, 22 Apr 2022)
correction: The quote is accurately reported. The fab, however, is TSMC Washington (formerly WaferTech, Fab 11) in the State of Washington. It started as a joint venture in 1996, with commercial production from October 1998 (TSMC 20-F FY2025), so it is not in Oregon and was not founded in 1997. The metric geography should read US (Washington State) vs Taiwan.
notes: Single tier-3 news source paraphrasing a talk. The '200mm' in the metric population is not in the article. New claim c_wafertech added for the fab facts.

original_interpretation: Morris Chang said in March 2023 that his earlier 50% estimate was an underestimate and US costs could be twice Taiwan's.
evidence_found: "Chang previously estimated that chip manufacturing costs in the US would be 50 percent higher than in Taiwan. 'I found out that was an underestimate.' ... Chipmaking costs in the US could be twice those in Taiwan, Chang said." (Taipei Times, 17 Mar 2023, p.1)
notes: Said at a CommonWealth Magazine forum. This is an executive opinion with no method behind it.

original_interpretation: Lisa Su said in July 2025 that TSMC Arizona chips would cost AMD more than 5% but less than 20% more than Taiwan chips.
evidence_found: "Su said AMD expects to receive its first chips from TSMC's Arizona fab by the end of the year, but noted they would be 'more than five percent but less than 20 percent'" higher in cost (DCD, 25 Jul 2025)
notes: The DCD body text dates the summit remark 'yesterday (June 23)', but the article is dated July 25, 2025 and links a Bloomberg story dated 2025-07-23, so July 2025 is correct. The metric's reading of this as the customer's cost (wafer price) is the researcher's own interpretation.

original_interpretation: Taipower raised industrial rates 12.5% on average from 16 Oct 2024 to an average NT$4.29/kWh; MOEA said this was still below South Korea's NT$4.65 in 1H24.
evidence_found: "hike electricity rates by 12.5 percent on average for industrial users" ... "industrial electricity rates would climb to NT$4.29 per (US$0.1355) unit on average, which is still lower compared with that of South Korea at NT$4.65 per unit in the first half of this year." ... "take effect from Oct. 16" (Taipei Times, 1 Oct 2024)
notes: NT$4.29 was the planned average at the time of the decision. A May 2026 CommonWealth op-ed (SRC-0714) gives the average actually paid as 'NT$4.27 per kilowatt-hour (kWh), held there since the last adjustment'. The rate in force afterwards is therefore about NT$4.27. This is a news source (tier 3) reporting an MOEA decision; a Taipower or MOEA primary source was not opened.

original_interpretation: A May 2026 CommonWealth op-ed asserted TSMC now pays more for power in Taiwan than at its US, Japan or German fabs after 25-39% industrial rate rises since 2024.
evidence_found: "Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC, ...) now pays more for electricity in Taiwan than at its US, Japanese or German fabs after industrial rate increases of 25–39% since 2024, while power for the system as a whole remains under-priced..." (CommonWealth op-ed by Romain Blachier)
correction: The column does make this assertion verbatim. The 'May 2026' date could not be confirmed on the page: the only date signal is a '202605' image upload path, and the browser hit a Cloudflare check. The same column also says Taiwan has 'the third-lowest industrial ... electricity rates in the world' and an industrial average of NT$4.27/kWh, which sits uneasily with the TSMC comparison.
notes: An outside author's opinion with no tariff data, so the assertion itself is unverified. The claim_type is better treated as reported_claim (what a column says) than interpretation.

original_interpretation: India's Cabinet approved (29 Feb 2024) the Tata-PSMC Dholera fab: Rs 91,000 crore, 50,000 WSPM, 28nm HPC and power-management chips.
evidence_found: "Tata Electronics Private Limited ('TEPL') will set up a semiconductor fab in partnership with ... PSMC ... Investment in this fab will be Rs.91,000 crore. ... Capacity: 50,000 wafer starts per month (WSPM)"; segments: "High performance compute chips with 28 nm technology", "Power management chips" (PIB, 29 Feb 2024)
notes: Official government release (tier 1). The investment figure is a planned project cost, not money already spent. The 300mm wafer size in the metric population is not stated in the release.

original_interpretation: The March 2025 FSA values the Tata Dholera fab at ₹91,526 crore, with ISM committing 50% pari-passu fiscal support for eligible costs.
evidence_found: Embedded ISM post: "FSA has been signed ... for Semiconductor Fab project worth ₹91,526 Cr. in Dholera, Gujarat"; body: "commands a total investment of over ₹91,000 crore ... The Government of India, through the India Semiconductor Mission, has committed 50% fiscal support on a pari-passu basis for eligible project costs" (PIB, 5 Mar 2025)
notes: The ₹91,526 Cr figure comes from the ISM social post embedded in the release; the release text itself says 'over ₹91,000 crore'.

original_interpretation: Tata Electronics stated the Dholera fab's total investment as up to INR 91,000 crore (~US$11bn).
evidence_found: "The fab construction will begin this year with a total investment of up to INR 91,000 crores (~US$11bn) and will generate over 20,000 direct and indirect skilled jobs in the region." (Tata Electronics release, Mumbai, 29 Feb 2024)
notes: Company statement (reported_claim). Note that the company says 'up to' while the March 2025 PIB release says 'over' ₹91,000 crore.

original_interpretation: ESMC Dresden expected to cost >€10bn and reach 40,000 300mm wafers/month on 28/22nm planar and 16/12nm FinFET.
evidence_found: "When fully operational, ESMC is expected to have a monthly production capacity of 40,000 300mm (12-inch) wafers on TSMC's 28/22 nanometer planar CMOS and 16/12 nanometer FinFET process technology ... Total investments are expected to exceed 10 billion euros consisting of equity injection, debt borrowing, and strong support from the European Union and German government." (TSMC PR, 20 Aug 2024)
notes: Planned capacity and investment ('when fully operational'), not actuals. The same release names the €5bn German state-aid measure.

original_interpretation: TSMC said (Feb 2024) that with fab 2 the overall JASM investment would exceed US$20bn, with fab 2 to begin operation by end-2027.
evidence_found: "to build a second fab, which is scheduled to begin operation by the end of the 2027 calendar year ... Together with JASM's first fab, which is scheduled to begin operation in 2024, the overall investment in JASM will exceed US$20 billion with strong support from the Japanese government." (TSMC PR, 6 Feb 2024)
notes: These are 2024 plans. TSMC's FY2025 20-F says 'Construction on the second site commenced in October 2025'. Press reports (not opened) suggest the fab-2 node and timing were being revised in 2026, so treat end-2027 as the original target.

original_interpretation: TSMC's Feb 2024 JASM release gave planned equity stakes of ~86.5% TSMC, 6.0% SSS, 5.5% DENSO, 2.0% Toyota.
evidence_found: "With this investment, TSMC, SSS, DENSO and Toyota will hold equity stakes of approximately 86.5%, 6.0%, 5.5%, and 2.0% in JASM, respectively. The closing of the transaction ... [is] subject to customary closing conditions." (TSMC PR, 6 Feb 2024)
notes: Accurate as a planned split. The realised stake is lower: 73% in the 2025 AR chart and '72.65%' in its director table (SRC-0731), and 'approximately 72.6%' as of 28 Feb 2026 in the 20-F (SRC-0825; new claim c_jasm726). CON-0067 updated. Do not use 86.5% as the current stake.

original_interpretation: METI minister said Japan would subsidise JASM fab 2 by up to ¥732bn, after up to ¥476bn for fab 1, ~¥1.208tn total (~40% of >US$20bn).
evidence_found: "Ken Saito, told the media ... that he would subsidize TSMC's second fab in Kumamoto by JPY732 billion (approximately US$4.9 billion)" ... "Nikkei reported that after directly subsidizing TSMC's first fab in Kumamoto by up to JPY476 billion ... for a total of about JPY1.208 trillion (about US$8 billion). That translates into a government direct subsidy percentage of 40%" (DIGITIMES, 26 Feb 2024)
correction: Only the ¥732bn figure for fab 2 is attributed to the METI minister, and DIGITIMES does not say 'up to' for it. The ¥476bn fab-1 ceiling and the ¥1.208tn total are attributed to Nikkei reporting. The 40% share is DIGITIMES' own calculation.
notes: Tier-2 trade press relaying Nikkei; no METI primary document was opened.

original_interpretation: CSIS reported Japan would subsidise up to one-third of capital costs for designated devices, equipment and materials, with conditions.
evidence_found: "The Japanese government has indicated that it will subsidize up to one-third of the capital costs incurred by domestic and foreign manufacturers to produce designated types of semiconductor devices ..., equipment, materials, and raw materials. The subsidies are conditioned on a minimum of 10 years of domestic production" (CSIS, Aug 2023)
notes: The CSIS piece is dated 'Published August 25, 2023'; the source publication_date was patched from 'unknown'. CSIS is a think tank describing government policy, and the METI programme text was not opened. The conditions are 10 years of domestic production and priority for domestic shipments in a shortage.

original_interpretation: The CHIPS award page lists TSMC Arizona expected capex of more than US$65bn for three greenfield leading-edge fabs in Phoenix.
evidence_found: "This funding will support TSMC's investment of more than $65 billion in three greenfield leading-edge fabs in Phoenix, Arizona"; Financial Summary: "Direct Funding Amount $6.6 billion ... Available Loan $5 billion ... Expected Capital Expenditure More than $65 billion" (NIST CHIPS page)
notes: This covers only the original three-fab award scope. The same page links a July 2026 NIST release saying TSMC's total planned US investment is now US$265bn (the original $65bn plus $100bn in March 2025 plus $100bn in July 2026). Do not read $65bn as TSMC's current total US plan.

original_interpretation: The CHIPS award page describes Micron's two-decade plan to invest ~US$100bn in New York and US$50bn in Idaho.
evidence_found: "This funding will support Micron's two-decade vision to invest approximately $100 billion in New York and $50 billion in Idaho"; Financial Summary: "Direct Funding Amount $6.44 billion; Expected Capital Expenditure Up to $150 billion over the next two decades" (NIST CHIPS page, Micron New York)
notes: Browser render of the page (web_extract returned only fragments). The page also links a June 2025 release on a US$200bn total Micron US commitment, so the $150bn covers only the NY+ID award scope. The plan is described as a 'vision'.

original_interpretation: Micron (Oct 2022) intends to invest up to US$100bn over 20+ years in a New York megafab, US$20bn first phase by end of decade, up to four 600,000 sq ft cleanrooms.
evidence_found: "Micron intends to invest up to $100 billion over the next 20-plus years to construct a new megafab in Clay, New York, with the first phase investment of $20 billion planned by the end of this decade." ... "The site could eventually include four 600,000 square foot cleanrooms" (Micron release PDF, 4 Oct 2022)
notes: The HTML release page is excerpted or behind Cloudflare, so the full text was read in the release PDF (added). The release also mentions US$5.5bn in New York State incentives.

original_interpretation: Samsung's minimum US$17bn Taylor investment splits into US$6bn buildings/real property and US$11bn machinery/equipment.
evidence_found: "Samsung plans to invest a minimum $17 billion in this build-out – $6 billion in buildings and other real property improvements, and $11 billion in machinery and equipment." (Samsung Semiconductor Taylor page, 'Economic Development Impact')
notes: Read in the browser; web_extract returned only fragments. This is the initial 2021 scope; Samsung's later Taylor plans and the CHIPS award are larger and are not covered by this claim.

original_interpretation: At its Nov 2021 announcement, Samsung's US$17bn Taylor fab targeted groundbreaking in 1H22 and operation in 2H24.
evidence_found: "Groundbreaking will be in the first half of 2022 with the target of having the facility operational in the second half of 2024." (Samsung Newsroom, 24 Nov 2021)
notes: Read via a direct HTML fetch, since web_extract and the browser timed out; the same text appears on news.samsungsemiconductor.com. This is a historical target that was missed (see CLM-1011: Fab 1 trial production expected around Sept 2026).

original_interpretation: Intel's Ohio press kit says Intel announced on 21 Jan 2022 an initial investment of more than US$28bn for two fabs in Licking County.
evidence_found: Press kit: "On January 21, 2022, Intel announced plans for an initial investment of more than $28 billion in the construction of two new leading-edge chip factories in Licking County, Ohio." Same page caption: "Intel announced plans in January 2022, to invest more than $20 billion". Original 21 Jan 2022 release: "an initial investment of more than $20 billion"
correction: The press kit does say >US$28bn, but what Intel actually announced on 21 January 2022 was 'more than $20 billion' (original release). US$28bn is a later revised estimate for the same two fabs. New claim c_ohio20 supersedes this one, and a contradiction record is added.
notes: Explains the US$20bn figure the researcher saw in search results. Intel later slowed Ohio construction (CLM-0946, CLM-2128).

original_interpretation: In June 2023 Intel said Magdeburg would need more than €30bn for two leading-edge fabs, with more German government support.
evidence_found: "The agreement encompasses Intel's expanded investment in the site, now expected to be more than 30 billion euros for two first-of-a-kind semiconductor facilities (also known as 'fabs') in Europe, along with increased government support that includes incentives" (Intel newsroom, 19 Jun 2023)
notes: Accurate as a historical statement, but the project is cancelled. Intel's Q2 2025 earnings release (24 Jul 2025, download.intel.com) says 'Intel will no longer move forward with planned projects in Germany and Poland' (also CLM-2128). Do not present €30bn as a live plan.

original_interpretation: Intel extended the useful life of certain production M&E from 5 to 8 years effective Jan 2023, estimated to raise 2023 gross margin by ~US$2.5bn.
evidence_found: "Effective January 2023, we increased the estimated useful life of certain production machinery and equipment from 5 to 8 years. When compared to the estimated useful life in place as of the end of 2022, we estimate this change increased gross margin in 2023 by approximately $ 2.5 billion and decreased R&D expense by approximately $ 400 million." (Intel 10-K FY2023, Note 6, Property, Plant and Equipment, EDGAR)
notes: The intc.com XBRL page (SRC-0729) showed only fragments, and the browser was refused connection, so the full text was checked in the EDGAR original (added). MD&A adds that total 2023 depreciation was reduced by $4.2bn. The $2.5bn is a company estimate inside an audited filing.

original_interpretation: Intel says its government incentives are mainly cash grants and refundable tax credits, with capital-related incentives running up to 15 years.
evidence_found: "These incentives are primarily structured as cash grants and refundable tax credits. Capital-related incentives have terms of up to 15 years and operating-related incentives have terms that can vary widely." (Intel 10-K FY2023, Note 6, Government Incentives, EDGAR)
notes: Verified in the EDGAR primary 10-K.

original_interpretation: TSMC depreciates M&E over 5 years and buildings over 10-20 years straight-line (2020 AR policy).
evidence_found: "computed using the straight-line method mainly over the following estimated useful lives: land improvements - 20 years; buildings (assets used by the Company and assets subject to operating leases) - 10 to 20 years; machinery and equipment ... - 5 years; and office equipment - 5 years." (TSMC 2020 Annual Report, p.183)
notes: The cited p.290 rendered only its title (web_extract) and was blocked by Cloudflare in the browser. The identical policy was confirmed on p.183 of the same report. It is still unchanged in the FY2025 20-F (new claim c_tsmclife25), so it is not outdated.

original_interpretation: TSMC Arizona 2025: net revenues NT$66.80bn, operating income NT$5.36bn, net income NT$16.14bn.
notes: The columns are capital stock, assets, liabilities, net worth, net revenues, operating income, net income and EPS. These are standalone subsidiary figures. Why net income exceeds operating income is not explained in the table.

original_interpretation: JASM 2025: net revenues NT$14.82bn, operating loss NT$14.21bn, net loss NT$9.77bn.
ESMC 2025: no revenue, net loss NT$0.69bn.
evidence_found: 8.1.6 (NT$ thousands): "European Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (ESMC) GmbH 42,553 82,240,527 25,847,937 56,392,590 0 (1,043,948) (688,621) (625.79)"
notes: The operating loss was NT$1.04bn.

original_interpretation: TSMC Nanjing 2025: net revenues NT$70.83bn, net income NT$27.61bn.
At end-2025 TSMC held 100% of TSMC Arizona, 73% of JASM and 70% of ESMC (2025 AR subsidiaries chart).
evidence_found: 8.1.1 chart: "Japan Advanced Semiconductor Manufacturing, Inc. Shareholding: 73% European Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (ESMC) GmbH Shareholding: 70%"; 20-F FY2025: TSMC Arizona is "a wholly-owned subsidiary"; "approximately 72.6% of the equity interest in JASM"; "we owned 70.0% of the equity interest in ESMC" (as of 28 Feb 2026)
notes: The Arizona line of the chart was cut from the extracted text, so the 100% was confirmed from the 20-F ('wholly-owned subsidiary'). The AR director table gives JASM as 72.65%; 73% is rounded.

original_interpretation: SK hynix (Feb 2026): total investment to build its first Yongin fab ~31tn won (~US$21.5bn) by end-2030, incl. 9.4tn won announced July 2024.
evidence_found: "invest approximately 21.6 trillion KRW (15 billion USD) in the new facility for the first fab by the end of December 2030. This brings the total investment for the construction of the first fab to approximately 31 trillion KRW (approx. 21.5 billion USD), which includes the approximately 9.4 trillion KRW ... previously announced in July 2024." (SK hynix, 25 Feb 2026)
notes: This is a company plan. It covers the fab shell and six cleanrooms, and the release does not say whether production tools are included.

original_interpretation: Seoul Economic Daily (Apr 2026): Samsung invested ~50tn won (US$36bn) building Pyeongtaek P4, a single fab with four cleanrooms on two floors.
evidence_found: "Samsung Electronics ... will bring its fourth plant (P4) at the Pyeongtaek campus into full operation within this year, having invested 50 trillion won ($36 billion) in its construction" ... "P4, which will house four cleanrooms across two floors, is currently operating at only half capacity" ... "P4 — a single fab receiving about 50 trillion won in investment" (SEDaily, 23 Apr 2026)
notes: The page notes it is 'AI-translated from Korean'. The figure is not confirmed by Samsung (tier-3 news), and 'estimate' is the right type. The same article puts P5 at more than 80tn won.

original_interpretation: SMIC signed (Aug 2022) a framework agreement to invest US$7.5bn in a 12-inch Tianjin line with 100k wafers/month for 28-180nm.
evidence_found: HKEX announcement (26 Aug 2022): "production capacity of 100,000 12-inch wafer per month (the 'Project'), providing wafer foundry and technology services on process nodes of 28 nanometer ~ 180 nanometer ... The Xiqing New Company shall have a registered capital of US$5 billion and the total investment sum in the Project will be US$7.5 billion."
notes: Checked against SMIC's primary HKEX filing (added) as well as the Reuters copy. The agreement is a planned 'cooperation framework agreement' and gives no production date.
